Depends on your needs. There's many different kinds of pistols (also certain rifles may even be a better choice if you're thinking home defense) and several calibers with different characteristics.

First, concealed or not? If you want to conceal then you need to take into consideration your size for potential pistols. I'm a small woman, so for on body carry I can't do much bigger than my MC1sc, but I also carry a purse so I can do off body with a larger gun. Men, typically, can conceal larger guns due to having a larger frame. Also take into consideration how you would prefer to carry concealed, some draw positions may not be conducive to larger pistols. However, if you're open carrying, disregard most of that and just find whatever you can reliably fit on your belt comfortably.

Next is caliber. Some calibers are more conducive to high rates of fire, while other pack more punch per shot. The standards right now are pretty much 9mm or .45, though .40S&W is certainly making gains as an intermediate(also i like it XD) and some people swear by .380, but its effectiveness teeters on the edge. Also, there's a ton of others that are well suited for self-defense, again just depends of preference. You also have to temper you caliber with your gun size. My compact 9mm has about as much kick as my full size .40 due to its lighter weight and shorter barrel. I also, at one time, had a compact .40 and .45 and they were almost unusable for me. So, basically, know what you can handle.

Also, as I said, for home defense (if that's what you're using the gun for) a carbine would be a good choice as well. There's short rifles in both pistol and rifle calibers that are superb for this function. The Keltec Sub2k is a folding light pistol caliber carbine, perfect for storage when not in use and very effective. Also, Keltec has the RDB which is a bullpup carbine in 5.56, very compact but still has a full length barrel, you might get lucky and find one for under 900, but the market is a little dry at the moment due to the pandemic. Of course, pretty much any shorter barrel (but not too short or you start getting into federal registration areas) ARs are common and good options.

Lasers like this have been around for a good decade now... at least back then, you could take the laser modules out of blu-ray DVD players and with the right electric parts, heat sink, and housing, people were fashioning these into multi watt blue lasers. To give you some point of reference, laser pointers in the US can't legally be over 5mW, or 5/1000 of a watt. You can have stronger lasers than that, but they must be for medical/research/laboratory purposes per their product description. Not surprisingly, a lot of really powerful green and blue pointers got around US regs by either being marketed in that way, or simply saying nothing about it being a laser pointer, rather calling them laser modules and wordplay like that.

We're talking stupidly dangerous power levels with these. Once you break past a few hundred milliwatts or so, you don't even have to have the beam pointed at your eye to cause permanent injury.... literally just looking at the "dot" will do it. These are light sources strong enough to illuminate an airplane high in the sky like it was hit by a spotlight (don't do this, its a felony). To add insult to injury, the price of these things has dropped MASSIVELY in the past 15 years, kindof like Moore's law did with circuitry. A 140mW green module cost me $450 back in 2005; you can now get several watt blue modules for a couple hundred bucks or less depending on quality.
